reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .416 xwOBA with a 2.69 xERA on the same Statcast card: there is no comparable profile in the sport. As a hitter, the contact quality is overwhelming — 17.1% barrel rate, 93.6 mph average exit velocity, and a 14.8% walk rate that shows he's working counts and taking what pitchers give him, though a 28.6% whiff rate means he can be beaten with swing-and-miss stuff. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball pairing with 27.9% strikeout rate and a barrel rate of just 3.8% against him explains why the xERA sits that low. The projection, .285/.396/.555 with 39 home runs across 685 plate appearances while also taking the ball as a starter, is less a forecast than a description of what happens when this profile stays healthy, which is the only dependency that matters.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-discipline split is the whole argument: a 17.4% walk rate paired with a 28.4% strikeout rate, which looks like a contradiction until you see the 22.0% chase rate sitting underneath it. He earns the walks by not expanding the zone, and the strikeouts come from swings he does take going wrong, not from getting fooled at the plate. When he connects, the .625 xSLG and 22.7% barrel rate suggest a hitter who punishes mistakes at a level that only a handful of big leaguers reach. The projection of 42 home runs with a .395 OBP in 732 plate appearances is the full translation of that Statcast profile, and the one dependency worth naming is whether that strikeout rate drifts further up as pitchers game-plan him more aggressively into his second full season.

reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six projected home runs from a 22-year-old, and the Statcast profile says believe it: 93.2 mph average exit velocity with a 51.8% hard-hit rate put him among the most dangerous contact makers in the sport. The .372 xwOBA and .505 xSLG aren't being dragged up by luck — a 12.9% walk rate keeps the denominator honest and a 19.0% strikeout rate means he's not burning at-bats to get there. The whole projection hinges on that plate discipline holding; if pitchers eventually find an exploit in his 28.8% chase rate, which is serviceable but not elite, the ceiling compresses. If it holds, this is a legitimate middle-of-the-order corner bat for a long time, OAA sitting at the bottom of the league and all.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .311, 100th percentile, tells you the contact quality is already pricing in what the .288 projection still treats as upside. Witt's 93.2 mph average exit velocity and 52.7% hard-hit rate are the engine, and the 33.2% chase rate is the one place the profile gives something back, keeping him from being an automatic on-base threat despite the raw power. Pair 24 home runs with 45 projected stolen bases at shortstop and you're describing a player who, if the plate discipline holds where it is rather than drifting, occupies the conversation about the best all-around position players in the sport without needing a leap in any tool. He's a franchise piece, and the Statcast profile says the production ceiling is still ahead of what he's done.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA (.364) and hard-hit rate (48.6%) say the contact quality is already elite-adjacent, but a 35.5% chase rate keeps this profile from being clean. What saves it is the walk rate: 11.2% is genuinely good, which means he's drawing enough free passes to partially offset the swing decisions, and the .864 OPS projection reflects that uneasy balance. If the chase rate drifts down even modestly over the next year, the .361 OBP and .503 projected slug stop looking like projections and start looking like a floor. Pair that contact profile with 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and 38 projected steals, and you have a 30-32 home run, 30-plus steal candidate who is one plate-discipline step away from being a middle-of-the-order anchor.

reports.name: Paul Skenes
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.71 and the walk rate at 5.5%, and together they describe a pitcher who earns his results rather than getting bailed out by them. Skenes strikes out 29.5% of batters while posting a contact-quality profile that holds hitters to a .258 xwOBA, which means the damage that does happen is mostly superficial. If the innings hold, he's a true staff ace before most pitchers his age have found their footing.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: impact everyday bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is impact over 232 PA.
reports.published_report: Thirty-eight stolen bases alongside a .415 OBP and an 18% walk rate is a profile that doesn't need context to read. The discipline translates well, a 12.3% walk rate against a major-league average of 8.5% in the MLB-equivalent conversion, and the ISO at .213 in the actual line comes with the caveat that it flattens to .14 against projected competition, roughly league-average pop, which means the impact ceiling depends on whether the raw power grows into the translation or stays there. reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.peak_summary: Projection: mid-rotation starter or better with low risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 72.7 IP.
reports.published_report: A 1.4 ERA over 72.7 innings at Double-A isn't a hot month, it's a full argument. Kade Anderson has walked 10 batters all season, and when that translates to MLB context, his projected BB/9 of 2.1 sits more than a full walk below the league average; the strikeout rate translates to 10.0 K/9 against an MLB average of 8.6. Every skill grade in the profile comes back 80, miss, command, dominance, run prevention, so the question isn't whether the stuff is there but whether a 21-year-old left-hander can hold this shape against better hitters as he climbs. If he does, the ceiling is a mid-rotation starter or better, and the floor is a multi-inning arm who still beats most MLB rosters.

reports.name: Juan Soto
reports.published_report: The .431 xwOBA is in the 99th percentile, and it sits next to a 19.9% chase rate and 16.5% walk rate that explain exactly how he gets there. Soto doesn't beat you with one skill; he makes contact on elite terms, walks at a rate barely any hitter in the sport matches, and barrels the ball 15.0% of the time. The projection, .284/.412/.553 with 36 home runs, is really just the Statcast profile translated into a counting-stat season, and the only thing keeping it from looking conservative is the sprint speed at 25.9 ft/s, which caps his baserunning upside and limits how much the 15 projected steals can grow. Everything else says frontline MVP candidate.

reports.name: Nick Kurtz
reports.published_report: The 18.4% walk rate is the highest in baseball, and it's doing real work against a 31.6% strikeout rate that would end most profiles before they started. What saves Kurtz is that the contact he makes is genuinely violent: 93.6 mph average exit velocity and 18.1% barrels put him in elite company on quality of contact, and the .379 xwOBA reflects that the damage is concentrated, not spread thin. The projection of .264/.395/.503 with 32 home runs lives or dies on whether he can keep chasing at just 22.8% as pitchers map his swing-and-miss; if that chase rate climbs, the strikeouts compound and the walks shrink, and a .503 slug turns into a much harder argument. Right now he's a middle-of-the-order bat hiding behind one of the ugliest whiff rates in the league, held together entirely by his eye and his power.

reports.name: Cody Bellinger
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is built on contact quality and discipline, not raw thump. His 12.7% walk rate pairs with a 14.9% strikeout rate, and that combination is why his xwOBA sits at .352 despite exit velocity and barrel rate that both land below the median. He makes enough contact at the right spots in counts to let the plate approach carry him, and the .277 xBA reflects genuine contact skill rather than soft-contact luck. The projection of .256/.340/.431 with 21 home runs across 662 plate appearances is the profile of a durable, useful regular whose value lives in the on-base column, and the power ceiling hinges on whether he can get his average exit velocity climbing; at 88.9 mph, there isn't a lot of margin left.

reports.name: Jackson Chourio
reports.published_report: The bat speed and raw thump are genuine: 92.2 mph average exit velocity, a 13.5% barrel rate, and an xSLG of .472 all point to a 22-year-old who already punishes mistakes at a level most hitters take years to reach. The tension is the chase rate. At 33.8%, he's swinging at pitchers' pitches often enough that the contact quality loses some of its weight in the walk column, and a 7.1% walk rate is what you'd expect from a hacker. The projection lands at .274/.326/.481 with 24 home runs and 16 steals, which is a legitimate everyday outfielder — the sprint speed at 28.7 ft/s keeps the profile well-rounded even when pitchers play cat-and-mouse in the zone. If the chase rate ever softens, this is a true middle-of-the-order bat; if it hardens, you're still looking at a productive regular, just one who always leaves something on the table.

Reynolds pairs that elite zone control, a 23.1% chase rate, with a 90.9 mph average exit velocity and a 47.3% hard-hit rate, producing an xwOBA of .369 that the projected .834 OPS more or less faithfully reflects. reports.name: Luis García Jr.
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .296, which is about as loud as a contact profile gets, and it's holding up because the chase rate is the real problem hiding in plain sight. García hits the ball hard, makes consistent contact when he swings, and the .511 xSLG translates into genuine over-the-fence power for a second baseman, all of which anchors ValuCast's projection of .280/.316/.518 with 29 home runs. But a 40.5% chase rate, the kind that lands in the bottom handful of the league, is the thing pitchers will keep selling him, and a 4.7% walk rate is the predictable result. If quality arms decide to live off the plate and he keeps biting, the strikeouts stay manageable but the on-base number never grows, and a .316 OBP is already thin for a lineup piece. The profile is a legitimate middle-of-the-order bat at second base as long as the contact holds, and a streaky, pull-heavy masher if the chase rate worsens.

reports.name: George Kirby
reports.published_report: The profile is built on an unusual foundation: elite command, modest strikeouts, and enough fastball to keep hitters honest. His 5.3% walk rate sits in the 93rd percentile among starters, but his 21.5% strikeout rate and 21.6% whiff rate are both below average, which means the margin for error is thin when contact happens. What saves him is how the contact lands: a 34.6% chase rate (88th percentile) gets him to weak swings on pitches outside the zone, and the 89.6 mph average exit velocity suggests he's genuinely limiting hard damage rather than running into soft contact luck. The projection of a 3.70 ERA over 179.6 innings holds if the chase rate stays where it is; if hitters start laying off those pitches, the low-whiff profile has nowhere to hide and the floor is a back-end starter surviving on defense and sequencing.

reports.name: Tyler Soderstrom
reports.published_report: That 13.0% walk rate is the load-bearing wall of this profile. Soderstrom controls the zone well enough to run a 25.6% chase rate while striking out just 17.6% of the time, which means contact is clean when he makes it, and the .343 xwOBA says he's earning those outcomes. The power is projectable rather than present — xSLG sits at .431 while ValuCast sees 25 home runs in a full season at .468 SLG, so some of that projection lives in the translation from expected to actual outcomes improving as he ages into his raw. The whole profile hinges on the walk rate holding; if pitchers find a way to exploit him and the chase number climbs, the .342 projected OBP craters and what's left is a first baseman with decent but not exceptional thump. Right now he profiles as a solid everyday regular with a real offensive floor.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan

His chase rate at 31.8% and whiff rate at 26.7% are legitimately above average, so the swing-and-miss profile hasn't vanished, but a 23.2% strikeout rate means he's not converting that deception into punchouts the way he once did. The projection's 3.20 ERA over 149.7 innings reads as optimistic against a Statcast card that doesn't yet support it, and the whole read hinges on whether the stuff behind that fastball velocity reasserts itself enough to push the strikeout rate back toward what he showed before the injury. If it does, he's a mid-rotation arm worth streaming; if it doesn't, the xERA is closer to who he is.

reports.name: Dylan Cease
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing standing between Cease and an argument for the best starter in the American League. His 36.9% strikeout rate and 35.9% whiff rate sit at the outer edge of what starters do in this league, and hitters are averaging 85.7 mph off him, which is what happens when barrels are almost entirely unavailable. The xERA of 2.84 and xwOBA of .264 are not aspirational — they describe what contact he has actually allowed. But 11.0% walks live in the bottom fifth of the league for starters, and every bad inning he has traces back to it; if the command doesn't tighten, the projection's 2.89 ERA and 1.15 WHIP require a lot of stranded traffic to survive. When it holds, he's a true number-one arm posting 239 strikeouts across 170 innings. When it slips, he's still very good, just noisier than the stuff deserves.

reports.name: Shota Imanaga
reports.published_report: The 37.4% chase rate is the engine of the whole profile, sitting at the 97th percentile among starters, and it explains why a guy throwing 91.8 mph can post a 3.74 xERA. His 2503 rpm on the fastball gives the pitch life that the velocity reading doesn't, and a 6.2% walk rate keeps hitters from simply waiting him out. The barrel rate of 10.2% is the thing to watch: he isn't missing barrels, and if his chase rate regresses even modestly, there isn't much velocity margin to absorb the damage. If the movement holds and hitters keep expanding, he's a mid-rotation workhorse; if the chase rate normalizes, the 4.10 ERA projection starts to look like a floor rather than a ceiling.

reports.published_report: A .327 average at 19 years old in full-season ball is the kind of number that makes you squint at the source, but 378 PA is a real sample. The contact rate grades out at the top of his peer pool, the 17% strikeout rate translates to roughly league-average at the MLB level, and he's added 18 stolen bases on top of a .506 slug, so the profile isn't just a batting-average mirage. The one thing to watch: his walk rate translates below the MLB mean, meaning the hit tool has to keep carrying the load, and if A-ball pitchers start attacking him differently and that average falls toward the .250s, the power (.122 ISO equivalent after translation) isn't enough to sustain an everyday profile on its own. If the bat plays, he's a low-end everyday center fielder within two to three years; if the contact slips and the walks don't grow, there's a bench role waiting at the floor.

reports.name: Frank Mozzicato
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 48.3 IP.
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud: 11.0 K/9 at AA, translating to 8.8 against a big-league average of 8.6. Everything else is a disaster. An 8.8 ERA, a 2.1 WHIP, and 47 walks against 59 strikeouts over 48.3 innings isn't a rough patch — it's a command profile that grades out at the 5th percentile among pitchers this year, and the MLB-equivalent walk rate of 6.4 sits well above the league norm of 3.2. The whole profile hinges on whether the miss-bat ability ever gets a command floor underneath it; right now those two skills aren't living in the same pitcher, and until that changes, the ceiling is a depth or relief role and the floor is the same thing.

O'Rae is walking at 16% while striking out at just 17%, and the MLB translation keeps that shape mostly intact: a projected 11.7% walk rate that clears the big-league average by a meaningful margin, with strikeouts projected below the MLB mean at 20.6%. The power is almost entirely absent, two home runs and a .095 ISO that grades at the 19th percentile among peers, and the translated .102 ISO sits well short of a league-average stick. reports.name: Nate Furman

reports.published_report: The contact rate is the whole argument here. Furman is running a 13% strikeout rate across 387 AAA plate appearances in 2026, and translated to MLB competition that holds at 16.7% while the average big-league hitter whiffs at 22.0%. The bat-to-ball is legitimate over a full-season sample, the .370 OBP suggests the approach grades out too, and 16 stolen bases tell you the profile has a way to create value beyond the box score. What it doesn't have is power: a .116 ISO at AAA that translates to .112 at the big-league level, well short of a league that averages .150, leaves him without a carry tool if the contact doesn't play up. If the hit and approach grades hold, he has a real shot at everyday utility; if MLB arms expose the soft profile, he's a useful bench piece who does a few things well.

reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the one thing that keeps this profile from being clean. Suzuki chases at 23.0%, which is genuine elite zone discipline, and he draws walks at 10.2%, but a 25.7% strikeout rate drags against both of those numbers and lands below the median for qualified hitters. Contact quality sits in the middle of the league, 89.0 mph average exit velocity and 40.6% hard-hit, yet his 9.2% barrel rate edges the contact into something more useful than those surface numbers suggest, and the .328 xwOBA reflects a hitter who gets more out of contact than the raw speed would imply. If the strikeouts stay where they are, he's a .261/.343/.454 everyday player who fits cleanly as a second-division regular; if they climb, the walk rate and barrel shape aren't enough to hold the floor.

reports.name: Ryan O'Hearn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is resolutely ordinary, except for one thing: O'Hearn gets to 44.9% hard contact without chasing, his 32.2% chase rate well below the league norm, and that combination is what drives a projection of .278/.345/.465 with 24 home runs over 568 plate appearances. The xwOBA (.333) and xSLG (.430) both land in the low-61st and 62nd percentiles respectively, which is exactly what a solid second-division regular looks like, not more, not less. Walk rate at 7.7% is below average, so the on-base value leans entirely on the bat making real contact, and if the hard-hit rate softens, the profile thins fast. A useful first baseman on a rebuilding Pittsburgh club, with a ceiling that's essentially what the projection already says.

reports.name: Tanner Scott
reports.published_report: A 3.5% walk rate from a reliever who already runs a 34.7% strikeout rate is the kind of combination that shouldn't exist, and yet here we are. Scott's chase rate sits at 40.7% and his whiff rate at 35.6%, which means hitters are swinging at the wrong pitches and missing them when they do — the 2.65 xERA is what you get when both things happen at once. The 2544 rpm spin on the fastball explains some of the bat-miss; the barrel rate of 6.8% is the one tick that's merely good rather than elite, and the projection absorbs that with a 2.85 ERA over 64.3 innings. Twenty projected saves for a Dodgers bullpen built on committee usage is probably a ceiling rather than an expectation, but the underlying profile makes the ERA look like a real floor.

reports.name: Troy Melton

reports.name: Gregory Soto

The strikeout rate at 27.0% is real enough to keep him in save situations, and a 3.85 ERA with 20 projected saves says he'll probably hold the Pittsburgh closer role, but the gap between what the contact profile deserves and what the walks give back is why you can't project him much beyond a mid-tier closer. If the command finds a floor, he's a steady 20-save reliever on a rebuilding club; if it doesn't, the xERA is noise and the blown opportunities pile up.

reports.name: Carlos Sanchez

The translated ISO comes in at .134 against a league mark of .150, so the raw power showing in the minors is going to blunt when it travels — the 10 home runs in the minors become something more modest in an MLB context, and the hit tool doing most of the heavy lifting is exactly what it will keep needing to do. reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest number in this profile. At 16% in 330 A-ball plate appearances, Arredondo draws walks at a clip that translates to 10.7% against an MLB average of 8.5%, and his approach grades 70 on the scale with an 83rd-percentile BB% to match. The K% sits at 18% at the level, becoming roughly 23.9% in translation, just a tick above average, but the BB-K balance is clean enough that a .389 OBP at 19 doesn't look like noise. Power is the dependency: his .152 ISO in A-ball shrinks to .113 in translation, well below the MLB mean, and if pull-side impact never develops against better arms, the approach alone probably caps him as a bench or platoon bat rather than an everyday third baseman. If it does develop, the 70-grade approach becomes a genuine weapon, and the ceiling is a regular.

reports.name: Carlos Rodríguez
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 319 PA.
reports.published_report: The contact rate is the whole argument here. Striking out just 10% of the time at AAA translates to a 15.1% K rate against MLB pitching, well below a league average that sits at 22.0%, which puts him in rarefied air among hitters at his level. The .302 average and .369 OBP over 319 PA are built on that contact skill plus a BB-K profile that comes out essentially even, and the 10 stolen bases add another dimension to what is otherwise a low-leverage offensive game. The hitch is the power: two home runs, an ISO of .089 in the minors that translates to .102 against MLB pitching, and a power grade well below average means his ceiling compresses sharply unless the gap power develops into something it hasn't shown yet. If the contact and speed hold and a little more pop arrives, a regular job is genuinely on the table; if the bat stays this gap-and-slap, he settles into a useful bench piece who can play center and put the ball in play when a lineup needs it.
